The Yellowback seabream (Evynnis tumifrons) is a commercially significant sparid inhabiting continental shelf waters of the northwestern Pacific. Early life stages exhibit traits typical of many marine teleosts, with females producing pelagic eggs following broadcast spawning events. Under controlled rearing conditions at a stable water temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], the interval from fertilisation to chorion rupture, or hatching, is approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days]. Newly emerged prolarvae are lecithotrophic and possess a prominent yolk sac that sustains them during the initial endotrophic phase. The wet weight at birth, measured immediately after eclosion, is 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], a minute mass reflecting the small dimensions of the ovum. This value corresponds to an egg diameter of approximately 0.85 mm, comparable to that recorded in congeneric sparids such as Diplodus sargus. Yolk absorption and mouth opening occur shortly thereafter, marking the onset of exogenous feeding and the transition to the pelagic larval phase.

As development proceeds, the growing juveniles exhibit a prolonged period of somatic investment before reaching sexual maturity. Field surveys and otolith-based back-calculation studies indicate that the total length at puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation, is 14.9 cm [Lp = 14.9 cm]. This length threshold is reached after several years of growth, depending on local environmental conditions and food availability. The attainment of reproductive maturity represents a significant life-history transition, after which individuals begin allocating resources toward gamete production. Prior to this point, energy is directed primarily toward increasing body size and building somatic reserves. The length-based maturity estimate aligns well with values reported for other small-bodied sparids sharing similar thermal habitats. Puberty is not strictly size-dependent in all populations, but the 14.9 cm [Lp = 14.9 cm] threshold serves as a reliable benchmark for the species across much of its geographic range.

Annual reproductive output in the Yellowback seabream is substantial, reflecting an iteroparous spawning strategy typical of the family Sparidae. Gravid females produce multiple batches of pelagic eggs over an extended spawning season. Under the prevailing thermal regime of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is achieved through a combination of clutch size and spawning frequency. Each spawning event yields approximately 221 eggs per batch [N_R_i = approximately 221 eggs per batch], and females typically produce a single batch each day [F_R_i = single batch each day] during peak spawning activity. This high-frequency, low-clutch-volume strategy maximises total fecundity over the breeding season. The daily reproductive output, derived from combining these two metrics, reaches approximately 221 eggs per day, a rate that is among the highest recorded for sparids of comparable body size. Such elevated fecundity is ecologically advantageous in an environment where egg and larval mortality are considerable.

Ultimate body size in Evynnis tumifrons is constrained by both genetic and environmental factors, with asymptotic growth attained after several years. The ultimate total length, derived from mark-recapture studies and length-frequency analysis, is 35 cm [Li = 35 cm]. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight associated with this maximum length reaches approximately 902 grams [Wwi = approximately 902 grams], a value calculated from a length-weight regression relationship (W = 0.02512 × L^2.95). This asymptotic mass represents the largest body size typically achieved by adults in wild populations, though occasional individuals exceeding this benchmark have been documented. The species exhibits moderate sexual size dimorphism, with females sometimes attaining slightly larger sizes than males. Growth trajectories decelerate markedly after the onset of reproductive maturity, as energy is increasingly diverted toward gamete production and spawning activities. The approximately 902 grams [Wwi = approximately 902 grams] adult mass positions the Yellowback seabream as an intermediate-sized sparid within its assemblage.

Longevity estimates for the Yellowback seabream are derived from captive rearing experiments and validated by otolith annulus counts from wild specimens. In controlled aquarium conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], which corresponds to roughly 5475 days. This extended longevity is consistent with a relatively slow life-history pace, characterised by delayed maturity, moderate fecundity, and sustained reproductive output over many spawning seasons. In wild populations, actual lifespan may be shorter due to fishing mortality and predation pressure, but the approximately 15-year ceiling (approximately 15 years) [am = approximately 15 years] provides an upper bound for demographic modelling at a temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C]. The species exhibits gradual senescence, with reproductive performance declining only in the oldest individuals. This lifespan is comparable to that of other temperate sparids such as Pagrus major and Acanthopagrus schlegelii, which similarly inhabit the East China Sea and adjacent waters.
